description: 'The proliferation of psychological databases worldwide has created an unprecedented opportunity for secondary data analysis using self-reported psychological assessments. Countries across the globe have established comprehensive databases containing psychological modules, including the UK Biobank, the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) covering 20 European countries, the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), China’s CHARLS(The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study), and emerging databases in resource-limited settings such as maternal health databases along the Myanmar-Thailand border. These databases predominantly rely on self-reported assessment tools to capture psychological data, generating a substantial volume of research publications indexed in PubMed and Web of Science that utilize secondary psychological self-assessment data.


  However, this rapid growth in database-driven psychological research has revealed significant reporting gaps that distinguish these studies from traditional primary data collection observational studies. Research utilizing secondary psychological self-assessment database data presents unique methodological challenges that require specialized reporting considerations. The reliance on pre-existing self-reported assessment tools introduces complexities regarding the validation and applicability of these instruments when applied to secondary database populations that may differ substantially from the original validation cohorts.


  Several critical reporting elements are consistently underreported in current literature. For self-assessment tools, particularly psychological scales, studies frequently fail to adequately report the reliability and validity evidence, the source and appropriateness of cutoff points, and whether these parameters were derived from the secondary database population or transferred from original literature populations. Database-specific methodological issues, such as approaches to handling bias when required covariates are unavailable in existing database variables, are often inadequately addressed. Additionally, psychological research, even in general population studies, requires reporting of population-specific contextual factors that may serve as confounders, including pandemic effects, addictive behaviors, and other psychological stressors that may not be routinely captured in standard epidemiological reporting.


  Currently, researchers in this field predominantly rely on general observational reporting frameworks such as STROBE. While these frameworks provide a useful foundation for observational research, they do not adequately address the specific methodological considerations involved in studies using psychological self-report instruments in large databases, particularly regarding the reporting of instrument validity, reliability, and the generalizability of findings derived from secondary data. This gap has resulted in inconsistent and often insufficient reporting of critical methodological details, limiting the ability of readers to assess study quality, replicate findings, and synthesize evidence across studies. The PRIDE reporting guideline aims to address these gaps by providing structured guidance for reporting studies using psychological self-report instruments in large databases.
